opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing would be seeing AI systems actually generate substantial economic value across a broad range of tasks, not just impressive benchmark results. Benchmarks have been saturating very quickly for years, but that hasn't translated into the kind of broad labor substitution you'd expect if we were close to AGI. So if I started to see AI revenues growing much faster than they currently are, say, AI companies' revenue doubling every few months and on track toward something like a meaningful fraction of world GDP, that would move me a lot.

A second thing is evidence that the hard parts are getting solved: agency, long-horizon coherence, and the ability to operate in messy, open-ended environments without constant human supervision. Current systems are very good at tasks that are well-specified and short, but they struggle when they need to manage a project over days or weeks, recover from their own mistakes, or deal with context that isn't neatly packaged for them. If we saw agents reliably doing multi-week tasks that a competent remote worker would do, things like running a small piece of a business end to end, that would be a big update.

Third, I'd look at whether progress depends less on scaling compute. A lot of my skepticism about very short timelines comes from thinking that we'll need a lot more compute, and compute scaling faces real constraints: chip production, energy, capital. If it turned out that algorithmic improvements alone could get us most of the way, or that some new paradigm gave dramatically better returns per unit of compute, then the bottlenecks I'm worried about would matter much less.

And finally, I'd want to see AI meaningfully accelerating AI research itself, not in the sense of writing some code faster, but actually substituting for top researchers in a way that visibly speeds up the field. If that feedback loop kicked in, it could compress timelines a lot. So far I don't think we're seeing that at a scale that changes the picture, but it's the kind of thing I'd watch closely.

r001.rationale: The response names agency and long-horizon coherence as current weaknesses and describes what successful agents would look like, but it does not identify a clear trend of improvement in those capabilities.

r002.rationale: It mentions a rate of AI revenue growth and compute efficiency, but does not say that expectations of AGI before 2030 depend on the rate of capability improvements.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention robotics or a robotics breakthrough.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing I'd want to see is evidence that the current paradigm can handle the kinds of tasks that we actually can't automate right now, and that it can do that without requiring enormous amounts of additional compute scaling.

So let me be a bit more concrete. Right now, if you look at where models are, they're very good at short-horizon tasks. If you give them a well-specified problem, something that would take a human maybe a few minutes, or in some cases a few hours, they can do that quite well. Where they fall down is on tasks that require operating over long time horizons, maintaining context, learning on the job, dealing with situations that aren't well represented in the training data. And a lot of economically valuable work is like that. It's not just answering a question, it's working on something for weeks or months, accumulating knowledge about the specific environment you're in, noticing when things are going wrong and correcting course.

So one piece of evidence would be seeing a model that can actually do that. Not on a benchmark, but in practice. If I saw a model that could be dropped into a software company, say, and over the course of a few months it got better at that job in the way a new hire does, that would update me a lot. Because that's the thing I think is missing, and I don't currently see a clear path to it from just scaling up what we have.

The second thing is the trend in how fast the time horizon of tasks that models can do is growing. There's this work from METR where they measure the length of tasks that models can complete with some reliability, and that's been doubling every seven months or so. If that trend continued, or especially if it accelerated, then you get to pretty long task horizons by 2030. But I'm somewhat skeptical that the trend will hold, partly because the tasks they measure are fairly clean and well-specified, and partly because I think a lot of the recent gains have come from things like reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, which might not generalize to messier domains. So if I saw the trend hold up on tasks that are much messier, much less well-specified, that would be meaningful.

And then the third thing is just the compute question. My view is that a lot of the progress we've seen has been driven by scaling compute, and compute scaling is going to slow down at some point because you run into constraints on energy, on chip manufacturing, on how much money people are willing to spend. If we got to the point where we could see the algorithms were clearly getting a lot more efficient, so that you didn't need the compute scaling to continue at the current pace, that would also move me. Right now I think a lot of the burden is being carried by compute, and that's a trend that I expect to run into limits before 2030.

So I'd say those three. Evidence of on-the-job learning and long-horizon agency in real environments rather than benchmarks, the task-horizon trend holding up in messy domains, and algorithmic progress that decouples capability gains from compute scaling. If I saw all of those, I'd probably put a substantially higher probability on AGI before 2030 than I do now. Right now I think it's possible, maybe something like a 10 to 20 percent chance, but my median is later than that.

r001.rationale: It points to growing task horizons, especially if that improvement continues or accelerates and holds up on messier tasks, as evidence that would raise the chance of AGI before 2030.

r002.rationale: It makes the forecast depend on whether the task-horizon trend continues or accelerates, citing a current doubling rate of about seven months.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention robotics or a sudden robotics breakthrough.

astra-6.text:
I think the strongest evidence would be AI systems becoming much better at doing long, complex tasks autonomously. There’s a big difference between answering a difficult question and taking a vaguely specified research problem, figuring out what to try, running experiments, and recovering when something goes wrong. If we saw systems reliably doing the latter, that would move me substantially toward AGI before 2030.

AI accelerating AI research would be particularly significant. Are these systems actually helping researchers make progress faster, and can they take on an increasing share of the work? You’d want to measure the overall effect, because being very good at writing code doesn’t necessarily mean you can drive a research project.

I’d also update if those improvements were predictable across successive generations of models. One impressive demonstration is weaker evidence than a sustained trend in how much useful work systems can do with less human supervision. If that trend were moving quickly enough, then a date before 2030 would become much more plausible to me.

r001.rationale: It points to sustained improvement in autonomous performance on long, complex tasks—an area described as a major gap—as evidence favoring AGI before 2030.

r002.rationale: It says the trend would make 2030 more plausible if it were moving quickly enough, making the rate of improvement relevant.

r003.rationale: It does not identify a sudden breakthrough in robotics as significant evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important evidence would be seeing AI systems reliably complete much longer tasks without human intervention. At the moment, there’s a big difference between doing well on a benchmark and being able to take a vaguely specified objective, work on it for a week, notice when you’ve made a mistake, and recover from it.

So, for example, if we saw systems that could independently do substantial software engineering projects, or carry out research where the outcome wasn’t already known, that would move me quite a lot. Especially if they could do this across a broad range of tasks, rather than in a few carefully selected demonstrations.

Another thing would be evidence that AI is substantially accelerating AI research itself. If these systems start making researchers much more productive, and that translates into faster improvements in the next generation of models, then you have a reason to expect the pace of progress to change.

I’d put less weight on a single impressive benchmark result. What I’d want to see is that the remaining limitations—reliability, learning new things, operating over long horizons—are actually going away, and that the improvements are happening fast enough to make a date before 2030 plausible.

r001.rationale: The response points to improvements in historically difficult capabilities, including reliable long-horizon work, learning new things, and recovering from mistakes, as evidence for AGI before 2030.

r002.rationale: It says the improvements must be happening fast enough to make a pre-2030 date plausible.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify a sudden breakthrough in robotics as significant evidence.
